# Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta (MN 14 (PTS MN i 91))

**ID:** MN 14 (PTS MN i 91)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering
**PTS:** MN i 91

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering", MN 14; PTS MN i 91) is set in the Sakyan country at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha's Park, where Mahānāma the Sakyan approaches the Buddha to ask why defiled states such as greed, ill will, and delusion can still overwhelm the mind despite long spiritual training [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Nattier, Guide to the Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations; SuttaCentral]. In response, the Buddha recounts his own pre-awakening realization as an unawakened bodhisattva that sensual pleasures offer little gratification and much dissatisfaction, explaining that sensual attachments cannot be abandoned without attaining the wholesome, blameless pleasure found in meditative absorption (*jhāna*) [Stanley et al. 2018; SuttaCentral; Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation].

The discourse then transitions into a confrontation between the Buddha and Jain ascetics (Nigaṇṭhas) practicing painful austerities, such as standing continuously without sitting [Polak 2011; Devdas 2004]. Following the teachings of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the Jains held that accumulated unwholesome kamma must be worn away (*nijjaretha*) through severe asceticism (*tapas*) and new actions prevented through physical, verbal, and mental restraint, asserting that happiness cannot be achieved through happiness but must be attained through pain [Bronkhorst 1993; Devdas 2004; Polak 2011]. The Buddha challenges their doctrine, demonstrating the impossibility of calculating karmic fruition and contrasting their painful mortification with his own ability to abide in meditative bliss for up to seven days—a happiness greater than that of King Bimbisāra [Devdas 2004; Anālayo 2017; Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation].

MN 14 shares an extensive passage on the dangers of sensual pleasures (§§6–14) verbatim with the preceding *Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta* (MN 13, §§7–15), as well as descriptions of Jain austerities with the *Devadaha Sutta* (MN 101) [Nattier, Guide to the Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations; DharmaNexus; Polak 2011]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus match the discourse with early Chinese parallels, including an early separate translation attributed to Zhi Qian (*Shi Monan ben sizi jing*, T 54), a discourse in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 100 / T 26), and one in the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 41.1 / T 125) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Nattier, Guide to the Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations; Nattier, Ten Epithets; Anālayo 2017]. DharmaNexus also confirms extensive internal Pali text reuse with the *Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa* (Cnd 23) and various discourses of the Aṅguttara and Saṁyutta Nikāyas [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
